newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Carter sees risk of South American arms race.
newsitem.headline: Carter sees risk of South American arms race.

text.p: South America could enter a new arms race if Chile goes ahead with a plan to purchase advanced fighter aircraft, former U.S. President Jimmy Carter said on Thursday.

Interest shown by Chile's armed forces in buying U.S. F-16 jets or similar advanced fighter aircraft from Europe would encourage neighbouring countries to increase defence spending, unsettling civilian rule in the region, Carter said.

"These supersonic aircraft will be a quantum leap and are very expensive. They would almost force Argentina and other neighbours to meet this new level of weaponry," he told reporters on a tour of South America that included Chile.
As president in 1977, Carter prohibited the United States from selling sophisticated weapons to the region, which was dominated by military dictatorships at the time.
With Latin America now almost completely under civilian rule, and lucrative contracts in the offering, some members of the Clinton administration have argued that the ban should be relaxed.

"The U.S. has not made a decision about the availability of the F-16s. My hope is that, building on harmony and peace and a committment to social progress...the (Chilean) leaders would restrain themselves and not take this decision," Carter said.
Defence officials in Chile say they have looked at various models of European fighter aircraft and would be interested in buying F-16s if the United States changed its policy.

While the country's relations with its neighbours are good, there is resentment in Chile and Argentina over a settlement to a border dispute in the cold wastes of Patagonia that has yet to be ratified by both countries' parliaments.

Carter, who is touring South America to prepare a meeting of regional luminaries at his Carter Centre in April, paid tribute to the region's growing committment to free trade but said problems, such as the military's influence in Chile and high unemployment in Argentina, had to be addressed.

"In Brazil I am still deeply troubled by human rights abuses like child labour, mistreatment of women, remaining evidence of racism, problems of rights of Indian people and I would say in particular, the abusive character of police," he said.
Cuba was the "notable exception" to democracy in Latin America, but the United States' attempts to stifle trade with Havana was a "terrible mistake," Carter said.

"The embargo of goods gives (Cuban leader Fidel) Castro an excuse for his own maladministration of economics. It makes him look like a heroic David fighting against an American Goliath and he doesn't deserve to be treated as a hero," he said.
